title: Telling what happened
job: A four-sentence account in the past
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: <four-sentence account, aham written once at most>

rules.text: An account is told with four little words at the front of its sentences: prathamam ('first'), tataḥ ('then'), anantaram ('after that') and ante ('in the end'). None of them takes an ending, and each sits exactly where English puts its own — which makes them the easy half of this module.

The hard half is agreement. Every -tavān and -tavatī in one account describes the SAME person, so all four participles fork together: a man's account is -tavān all the way through and a woman's is -tavatī all the way through. Halfway is not a mistake of style; it is an account that nobody could have told.

The fork is on whoever the account is ABOUT, not on whoever is listening. When you are telling your own story that is you, so a woman says gatavatī even to a man; when the story is about somebody else, the participle follows them.

aham belongs in at most the FIRST sentence of an account, and usually in none of them. The -mi and the participle have already said who is speaking, and an account that opens every sentence with aham is grammatical and audibly wrong — it is the loudest anglophone tell this course can fix.

tataḥ is one letter from M9's ataḥ ('so') and shares its shape with six other little words this course owns: kutaḥ, yataḥ, purataḥ, pṛṣṭhataḥ, vāmataḥ, dakṣiṇataḥ and agrataḥ. They are separate words with separate meanings, and swapping one for another builds a perfectly grammatical sentence that says something else.

There is still no imperfect and there is still no bare participle. M8's ruling holds to the last account of the level: abhavat is written nowhere, and gataḥ, kṛtam and naṣṭam are written nowhere. An account wants them more than any other module and does not get them.

The account's verbs are L1's, every one: gatavān, khāditavān, paṭhitavān, likhitavān, kṛtavān and pītavān, each with its -tavatī twin. This module opens four small words and reuses everything else, which is what makes it the test of the level rather than an addition to it.

M9's yataḥ ('because') and ataḥ ('so') can sit inside an account, and M10's ca, kintu, tathāpi and api can join its clauses. An account is not a special kind of sentence; it is four ordinary ones in a row.

Each sentence in an account is closed before the next begins. English runs an account together with 'and then' and 'after that I'; here every sentence ends, and the sequencer at the front of the next one is the whole of the join.

The account can be told in the future with exactly the same four words: śvaḥ prathamam vidyālayam gamiṣyāmi, tataḥ saṃskṛtam paṭhiṣyāmi. The sequencers know nothing about tense, and this is the cheapest thing in the module.

sentences.display: prathamam aham vidyālayam gatavān. tataḥ saṃskṛtam paṭhitavān. anantaram gṛham gatavān. ante bhojanam khāditavān.
sentences.script: प्रथमम् अहम् विद्यालयम् गतवान्। ततः संस्कृतम् पठितवान्। अनन्तरम् गृहम् गतवान्। अन्ते भोजनम् खादितवान्।
sentences.cue: First I went to the school. Then I studied Sanskrit. After that I went home. In the end I had a meal.
sentences.literal: first I school-to went. then Sanskrit read. after-that home-to went. in-the-end meal ate

words.note: 'First', opening an account. It takes no ending and never changes shape, and it sits at the very front of its sentence where English puts it too.
'Then'. It is one letter from M9's ataḥ ('so') and it is a different word: tataḥ orders events, ataḥ draws a conclusion.
M2's verb of going, here as gatavān — the past M5 settled for the whole course. It agrees with the speaker, so a woman says gatavatī.

sentences.trap: Four sentences and one aham. English repeats the subject in every clause, and here the participle's ending has already said who did it — writing aham four times is the single most audible mistake this module can produce.
sentences.sound: pra-tha-MAM a-HAM vid-YAA-la-yam GA-ta-vaan. TA-tah sams-KRI-tam PA-thi-ta-vaan. The sequencer is said first and a little apart from what follows it.

variations.display: prathamam aham vidyālayam gatavatī. tataḥ saṃskṛtam paṭhitavatī. anantaram gṛham gatavatī. ante bhojanam khāditavatī.
variations.script: प्रथमम् अहम् विद्यालयम् गतवती। ततः संस्कृतम् पठितवती। अनन्तरम् गृहम् गतवती। अन्ते भोजनम् खादितवती।
variations.cue: First I went to the school. Then I studied Sanskrit. After that I went home. In the end I had a meal.
variations.changed: the whole account is told by a woman, so ALL FOUR participles fork to -tavatī — this is the variation that matters most in this module

variations.display: prathamam aham vidyālayam gatavān. tataḥ saṃskṛtam paṭhitavān. ante gṛham gatavān.
variations.script: प्रथमम् अहम् विद्यालयम् गतवान्। ततः संस्कृतम् पठितवान्। अन्ते गृहम् गतवान्।
variations.cue: First I went to the school. Then I studied Sanskrit. In the end I went home.
variations.changed: the account shortens to three sentences and anantaram simply drops; four is the shape, not a quota

variations.display: śvaḥ prathamam vidyālayam gamiṣyāmi. tataḥ saṃskṛtam paṭhiṣyāmi. ante gṛham gamiṣyāmi.
variations.script: श्वः प्रथमम् विद्यालयम् गमिष्यामि। ततः संस्कृतम् पठिष्यामि। अन्ते गृहम् गमिष्यामि।
variations.cue: Tomorrow I will go to the school first. Then I will study Sanskrit. In the end I will go home.
variations.changed: the same account in the future, with the same four sequencers and L1's -ṣyāmi endings — the little words know nothing about tense

mistake.display: prathamam aham vidyālayam gatavān. tataḥ aham saṃskṛtam paṭhitavān. anantaram aham gṛham gatavān. ante aham bhojanam khāditavān.
mistake.why: Every sentence is grammatical and the account is wrong. aham belongs in the first sentence at most; the -tavān on each verb has already said who is speaking, and repeating the pronoun four times is the English habit showing through.

sentences.usage: The plainest account this course can tell: a day in four sentences.
sentences.mnemonic: prathamam, tataḥ, anantaram, ante. First, then, after that, in the end — four words in the order they will always come.

sentences.display: prathamam aham pustakālayam gatavatī. tataḥ pustakam paṭhitavatī. anantaram gṛham gatavatī. ante jalam pītavatī.
sentences.script: प्रथमम् अहम् पुस्तकालयम् गतवती। ततः पुस्तकम् पठितवती। अनन्तरम् गृहम् गतवती। अन्ते जलम् पीतवती।
sentences.cue: First I went to the library. Then I read a book. After that I went home. In the end I drank some water.
sentences.literal: first I library-to went. then book read. after-that home-to went. in-the-end water drank

words.note: 'After that'. It is the longest of the four sequencers and the one that carries the middle of an account, and like the others it takes no ending.
'In the end', closing an account. It is what tells a listener the story is finishing, and nothing else in the four sentences does.
Here as gatavatī, because a woman is telling the account. This is the same one row M2 opened, and the fork is on the person and not on the verb.

sentences.trap: The whole account is feminine because one person is telling it. Nothing in the story is about a woman except the person speaking, and that is enough to decide all four endings.
sentences.sound: pra-tha-MAM a-HAM pus-ta-KAA-la-yam GA-ta-va-tee. AN-te JA-lam PEE-ta-va-tee. The -vatī ending is three light beats and the final one is long.

variations.display: prathamam aham pustakālayam gatavān. tataḥ pustakam paṭhitavān. anantaram gṛham gatavān. ante jalam pītavān.
variations.script: प्रथमम् अहम् पुस्तकालयम् गतवान्। ततः पुस्तकम् पठितवान्। अनन्तरम् गृहम् गतवान्। अन्ते जलम् पीतवान्।
variations.cue: First I went to the library. Then I read a book. After that I went home. In the end I drank some water.
variations.changed: the same account told by a man, with all four participles forking the other way

variations.display: prathamam aham pustakālayam gatavatī. tataḥ pustakam paṭhitavatī. anantaram gṛham gatavatī. ante dugdham pītavatī.
variations.script: प्रथमम् अहम् पुस्तकालयम् गतवती। ततः पुस्तकम् पठितवती। अनन्तरम् गृहम् गतवती। अन्ते दुग्धम् पीतवती।
variations.cue: First I went to the library. Then I read a book. After that I went home. In the end I drank some milk.
variations.changed: the last thing drunk changes and no ending moves, because a noun in this slot never touched the participle

variations.display: prathamam sā pustakālayam gatavatī. tataḥ pustakam paṭhitavatī. anantaram gṛham gatavatī. ante jalam pītavatī.
variations.script: प्रथमम् सा पुस्तकालयम् गतवती। ततः पुस्तकम् पठितवती। अनन्तरम् गृहम् गतवती। अन्ते जलम् पीतवती।
variations.cue: First she went to the library. Then she read a book. After that she went home. In the end she drank some water.
variations.changed: the account is about somebody else — 'she' — so sā appears once and the participles stay -tavatī

sentences.usage: A woman's account of the same kind of day, and the one to read straight after the first.

sentences.display: hyaḥ prathamam jalam pītavān. tataḥ phalam khāditavān. anantaram saṃskṛtam likhitavān. ante aham santuṣṭaḥ.
sentences.script: ह्यः प्रथमम् जलम् पीतवान्। ततः फलम् खादितवान्। अनन्तरम् संस्कृतम् लिखितवान्। अन्ते अहम् सन्तुष्टः।
sentences.cue: Yesterday I first drank some water. Then I ate a fruit. After that I wrote Sanskrit. In the end I was content.
sentences.literal: yesterday first water drank. then fruit ate. after-that Sanskrit wrote. in-the-end I content

words.note: Ordering the second event. Notice hyaḥ at the very front: a time word fixes the whole account, and the sequencers then order what happened inside it.
M4's verb of drinking, here as pītavān. That module shipped the participle and this one only arranges it.
M5's 'yesterday'. One time word at the head of an account covers all four sentences, and repeating it in each would be as wrong as repeating aham.

sentences.trap: hyaḥ is said once and governs four sentences. English would put 'yesterday' in the first clause and then rely on the tense; here the participles are not a tense, so the time word carries the day on its own.

variations.display: hyaḥ prathamam jalam pītavatī. tataḥ phalam khāditavatī. anantaram saṃskṛtam likhitavatī. ante aham santuṣṭā.
variations.script: ह्यः प्रथमम् जलम् पीतवती। ततः फलम् खादितवती। अनन्तरम् संस्कृतम् लिखितवती। अन्ते अहम् सन्तुष्टा।
variations.cue: Yesterday I first drank some water. Then I ate a fruit. After that I wrote Sanskrit. In the end I was content.
variations.changed: the whole account told by a woman, ending in santuṣṭā — the adjective forks with the participles because it describes the same person

variations.display: hyaḥ prathamam jalam pītavān. tataḥ phalam khāditavān. ante saṃskṛtam likhitavān.
variations.script: ह्यः प्रथमम् जलम् पीतवान्। ततः फलम् खादितवान्। अन्ते संस्कृतम् लिखितवान्।
variations.cue: Yesterday I first drank some water. Then I ate a fruit. In the end I wrote Sanskrit.
variations.changed: three sentences instead of four, with anantaram dropped and the story none the worse

variations.display: hyaḥ prathamam jalam pītavān. tataḥ phalam khāditavān. anantaram saṃskṛtam likhitavān. ante aham khinnaḥ.
variations.script: ह्यः प्रथमम् जलम् पीतवान्। ततः फलम् खादितवान्। अनन्तरम् संस्कृतम् लिखितवान्। अन्ते अहम् खिन्नः।
variations.cue: Yesterday I first drank some water. Then I ate a fruit. After that I wrote Sanskrit. In the end I was downcast.
variations.changed: the ending reverses: M9's khinnaḥ in place of santuṣṭaḥ, and nothing before it moves

mistake.display: hyaḥ prathamam jalam pītavān. ataḥ phalam khāditavān. anantaram saṃskṛtam likhitavān. ante aham santuṣṭaḥ.
mistake.why: ataḥ has been written for tataḥ. It is a real word — M9's 'so, therefore' — and the sentence it makes is perfectly grammatical: 'so I ate a fruit'. It just is not what the account meant, and no test anywhere will catch it.

sentences.usage: An account that ends in how you felt rather than in what you did, which is the commonest way an account ends.

sentences.display: prathamam rāmaḥ vidyālayam gatavān. tataḥ saḥ saṃskṛtam paṭhitavān. anantaram gṛham gatavān. ante phalam khāditavān.
sentences.script: प्रथमम् रामः विद्यालयम् गतवान्। ततः सः संस्कृतम् पठितवान्। अनन्तरम् गृहम् गतवान्। अन्ते फलम् खादितवान्।
sentences.cue: First Rāma went to the school. Then he studied Sanskrit. After that he went home. In the end he ate a fruit.
sentences.literal: first Rāma school-to went. then he Sanskrit read. after-that home-to went. in-the-end fruit ate

words.note: Opening an account about somebody else. The sequencers do not care whose story it is.
M1's name as the subject of the account. He is named once, in the first sentence, and the participles carry him through the other three.
M5's 'he', written once for clarity and dropped in the last two sentences. The same economy that governs aham governs this word.

sentences.trap: The participles are masculine because RĀMA is a man, not because the speaker is. When an account is about somebody else, the fork follows them.
sentences.sound: pra-tha-MAM RAA-mah vid-YAA-la-yam GA-ta-vaan. Said flatly, as a report rather than a story.

variations.display: prathamam sītā vidyālayam gatavatī. tataḥ sā saṃskṛtam paṭhitavatī. anantaram gṛham gatavatī. ante phalam khāditavatī.
variations.script: प्रथमम् सीता विद्यालयम् गतवती। ततः सा संस्कृतम् पठितवती। अनन्तरम् गृहम् गतवती। अन्ते फलम् खादितवती।
variations.cue: First Sītā went to the school. Then she studied Sanskrit. After that she went home. In the end she ate a fruit.
variations.changed: the account is about Sītā, so every participle forks with her

variations.display: prathamam rāmaḥ vidyālayam gatavān. tataḥ saṃskṛtam paṭhitavān. anantaram gṛham gatavān. ante phalam khāditavān.
variations.script: प्रथमम् रामः विद्यालयम् गतवान्। ततः संस्कृतम् पठितवान्। अनन्तरम् गृहम् गतवान्। अन्ते फलम् खादितवान्।
variations.cue: First Rāma went to the school. Then he studied Sanskrit. After that he went home. In the end he ate a fruit.
variations.changed: saḥ drops from the second sentence, which is what a speaker actually does once the subject is established

variations.display: prathamam aham vidyālayam gatavān. tataḥ saṃskṛtam paṭhitavān. anantaram gṛham gatavān. ante phalam khāditavān.
variations.script: प्रथमम् अहम् विद्यालयम् गतवान्। ततः संस्कृतम् पठितवान्। अनन्तरम् गृहम् गतवान्। अन्ते फलम् खादितवान्।
variations.cue: First I went to the school. Then I studied Sanskrit. After that I went home. In the end I ate a fruit.
variations.changed: the account becomes the speaker's own, so rāmaḥ and saḥ both give way to a single aham

sentences.usage: An account given about a third person — what somebody else did today.

sentences.display: prathamam sītā pustakālayam gatavatī. tataḥ sā pustakam paṭhitavatī. anantaram gṛham gatavatī. ante dugdham pītavatī.
sentences.script: प्रथमम् सीता पुस्तकालयम् गतवती। ततः सा पुस्तकम् पठितवती। अनन्तरम् गृहम् गतवती। अन्ते दुग्धम् पीतवती।
sentences.cue: First Sītā went to the library. Then she read a book. After that she went home. In the end she drank some milk.
sentences.literal: first Sītā library-to went. then she book read. after-that home-to went. in-the-end milk drank

words.note: Closing an account about somebody else. It is the only one of the four that tells a listener to stop expecting more.
M1's name. Naming her once at the head of the account is what sets all four participles to -tavatī.
M5's 'she', standing in for the name in the second sentence and dropped thereafter.

sentences.trap: The gender of this account was decided by one word in the first sentence, and four verbs three sentences later still obey it. Nothing in the last sentence says who is being talked about at all.

variations.display: prathamam rāmaḥ pustakālayam gatavān. tataḥ saḥ pustakam paṭhitavān. anantaram gṛham gatavān. ante dugdham pītavān.

variations.cue: First Rāma went to the library. Then he read a book. After that he went home. In the end he drank some milk.
variations.changed: the same account about a man, with all four participles forking together

variations.cue: First Sītā went to the library. Then she read a book. In the end she drank some milk.
variations.changed: three sentences, with anantaram dropped and the account still whole

variations.cue: First my sister went to the library. Then she read a book. After that she went home. In the end she drank some milk.

mistake.display: prathamam sītā pustakālayam gatavatī. tataḥ sā pustakam paṭhitavān. anantaram gṛham gatavatī. ante dugdham pītavān.
mistake.why: Two of the four participles have forked one way and two the other. Every sentence here is grammatical on its own and the account is impossible: it would have to be about two different people who are also the same person. This is the defect this module exists to prevent.

sentences.usage: The companion of the account before it, and the pair is what makes the fork visible.

sentences.display: prathamam aham yānena vidyālayam gatavān. tataḥ saṃskṛtam paṭhitavān. anantaram saṃskṛtam likhitavān. ante gṛham gatavān.
sentences.script: प्रथमम् अहम् यानेन विद्यालयम् गतवान्। ततः संस्कृतम् पठितवान्। अनन्तरम् संस्कृतम् लिखितवान्। अन्ते गृहम् गतवान्।
sentences.cue: First I went to the school by vehicle. Then I studied Sanskrit. After that I wrote Sanskrit. In the end I went home.
sentences.literal: first I by-vehicle school-to went. then Sanskrit read. after-that Sanskrit wrote. in-the-end home-to went

words.note: The third sequencer, carrying the middle of a longer day. Two ordinary sentences between prathamam and ante are what an account is.
M4's vehicle in its by-shape, yānena. An instrumental sits inside an account exactly as it sits inside any other sentence.
M4's road. It is not in this account and its by-shape mārgeṇa is in the second variation, which is how the two instrumentals of that module differ.

sentences.trap: The instrumental appears once, in the first sentence, and the other three sentences do not repeat it. How you travelled is said when you say you travelled, and not again.
sentences.sound: pra-tha-MAM a-HAM YAA-ne-na vid-YAA-la-yam GA-ta-vaan. yānena is four beats with the long aa held at the front.

variations.display: prathamam aham yānena vidyālayam gatavatī. tataḥ saṃskṛtam paṭhitavatī. anantaram saṃskṛtam likhitavatī. ante gṛham gatavatī.

variations.cue: First I went to the school by vehicle. Then I studied Sanskrit. After that I wrote Sanskrit. In the end I went home.
variations.changed: the whole account told by a woman, with all four participles forking

variations.display: prathamam aham mārgeṇa vidyālayam gatavān. tataḥ saṃskṛtam paṭhitavān. anantaram saṃskṛtam likhitavān. ante gṛham gatavān.
variations.script: प्रथमम् अहम् मार्गेण विद्यालयम् गतवान्। ततः संस्कृतम् पठितवान्। अनन्तरम् संस्कृतम् लिखितवान्। अन्ते गृहम् गतवान्।
variations.cue: First I went to the school along the road. Then I studied Sanskrit. After that I wrote Sanskrit. In the end I went home.
variations.changed: M4's other instrumental, mārgeṇa, replaces yānena — by the road rather than by vehicle

variations.display: prathamam aham yānena vidyālayam gatavān. tataḥ saṃskṛtam paṭhitavān. ante gṛham gatavān.
variations.script: प्रथमम् अहम् यानेन विद्यालयम् गतवान्। ततः संस्कृतम् पठितवान्। अन्ते गृहम् गतवान्।
variations.cue: First I went to the school by vehicle. Then I studied Sanskrit. In the end I went home.

words.note: Closing the account. Four sentences and four events, one sequencer each, is the shape this module is teaching.

comprehensionPool.cue: First my mother made the food. Then she drank some water. After that she read a book. In the end she was content.
